extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical essays; educated general readership
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for writing clear, public-spirited periodical essays and for choosing tone, style, and authorial candour; rooted in 18th-century Spectator essays but applicable to essayistic creative non‑fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate knowledge publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: Against the maxim 'Scire tuum nihil est nisi te scire hoc sciat alter' (A Man's Knowledge is worth nothing, if he communicates what he knows to any one besides). The author rejects the idea that knowledge should be hoarded and argues for publishing discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make your discoveries and thoughts public for the benefit of others; communicating knowledge is a natural pleasure and carries its own reward because forming ideas into words clarifies them and allows their truth to be tested by effects on readers. Avoid treating learning as an exclusive commodity reserved for elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write intelligibly; avoid affected obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not imitate those who affect obscurity (e.g. Persius) or the 'Moderns' who 'write without any Meaning at all' by throwing words at random and leaving readers to find sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear expression over deliberate opacity. The essay condemns the art of writing unintelligibly as an attempt to seem learned or to gain reputation. Examples/antipatterns: obscurity to conceal ignorance; composing sentences full of words but no meaning; the Egyptian 'Dark-Lanthorn' image as a person who keeps knowledge to himself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure writing has real meaning and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid producing elegant-sounding prose that lacks substantive meaning; don't 'write without any Meaning at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every period and phrase ought to convey thought; resist the temptation to use verbal fireworks or loose accumulations of words merely to appear abstruse. A meaningful paraphrase or faithful paraphrase that preserves the 'sublime, heavenly spirit' is preferable to a bland or low-spirited line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity reveals truth and improves the writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting thoughts into words shows whether they are just or false, and the process of expression improves the person who practices it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear prose to test and refine ideas; the reaction and understanding of readers is the true measure of an idea's soundness. Writing should be an instrument of self-improvement and public instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer cheerfulness as a habitual tone over transient mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: Chearfulness is a fixed, permanent habit of mind distinct from short, transient mirth; it keeps judgment undisturbed and prevents deep melancholy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a steady, composed, grateful tone in writing (especially moral or philosophical essays) rather than aiming merely for witty flashes. Portray or cultivate characters with even temper, serenity, and an inward cheerfulness that produces goodwill in readers; avoid portraying cheerfulness as frivolous or excessive mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tone that benefits self, readers, and moral ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheerfulness has three relations: to the self (clarity of imagination and judgment), to others (produces love and goodwill), and to the divine (implicit praise and gratitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing tone, consider these broader effects: a composed tone aids reasoning, endears the writer to readers, and expresses moral gratitude. This argues for temperate, philosophic prose in moral writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be candid about authorship and acknowledge faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Candour — acknowledging one's errors or true role (e.g., admitting one is 'barely the Publisher') — is honorable and produces inward ease; false claims of credit harm the conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In editorial practice and authorial statements, prefer honesty about contributions. Acknowledging faults gracefully can repair offences and is a mark of generous spirit; ostentation or stubbornly persisting in error is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary style appropriately: elegant, argumentative, or sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator 'writes often in an Elegant, often in an Argumentative, and often in a Sublime Style, with equal Success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be adaptable in style—use elegance for polished reflection, argumentation for persuasive pieces, and sublimity where loftier or elevated feeling is required—so long as each mode serves the subject. Successful essays may combine these registers when apt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using obscurity to elevate reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors affect an abstruse style to gain reputation ('they may be still more abstruse, to write without any Meaning at all'), or to reserve 'Arcana' for the great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use complexity or obscurity as a social signal of superiority. Reserve technical opacity only where genuine difficulty demands it; otherwise prefer plain language that lets merit, not mystery, establish reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid anecdote and concrete example to teach
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays use illustrative stories (Rosicrucius's sepulchre, the soldier kissing the stirrup, the waterman with a wooden leg) to make moral points memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ striking, concrete examples and short narratives to embody abstract principles and to engage readers' imaginations; anecdotes should illuminate the lesson rather than merely decorate prose.
